header: Date: 2027-10-14 | Time: 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Miles (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (NovaPay), Liam O'Connor (NovaPay), Sara Mu (NovaPay)
summary: Weekly POC sync to review throughput test results and tune batching/concurrency targets. Identified sustained throughput improvement using continuous batching and prefix caching, but saw p99 spikes at high concurrency. Action items: run longer concurrency sweep, share production traces, and deliver cost/latency tradeoffs for Dedicated pool options.
topics: Results from last week's throughput run
Continuous batching window and KV/prefix cache hit rates
Next steps and benchmarks to run
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is the weekly NovaPay POC sync. We'll go through the throughput runs Jordan sent, a quick recap and then tuning suggestions.
[00:12] Priya Patel: Thanks Alex, morning all. We had the team watching the last run — saw some good numbers but there's still a weird jitter at the high tail.
[00:22] Jordan Miles: yep so I ran the 8-32 concurrency passes with the continuous batching window set to 20ms, and KV cache warmup at about 70% hit-rate. The aggregate tokens/sec looked solid but p99 popped around 650ms at the 32 concurrency point.
[00:36] Liam O'Connor: yeah that's the thing we saw in prod-ish, when we burst it the queue length grows and then p99 degrades, even though average latency is okay.
[00:48] Sara Mu: quick clarifying q — when you say KV cache are you referring to prefix caching or full key-value? We call it prefix cache in our infra.
[00:55] Jordan Miles: sorry bad phrasing there — it's the prefix / KV cache for decoder states. Sometimes the transcript, uh, the notes say K V cash which is fun. The prefix hit-rate is the metric we tracked.
[01:06] Alex Chen: no worries. Okay first slide — throughput summary. Jordan, can you read the numbers you uploaded?
[01:12] Jordan Miles: sure, so baseline (no batching) at concurrency 8 gave ~1.2k tokens/sec with p95 ~120ms p99 ~280ms. With continuous batching (20ms window) at concurrency 8 we hit ~2.1k tokens/sec. At concurrency 16 we saw ~3.9k tokens/sec but p99 jumped to ~420ms. At concurrency 32 best-case tokens/sec ~6.8k but p99 up to ~650ms as I said.
[01:34] Priya Patel: those are good gains but our SLO is p99 < 500ms for user requests. So 650 is outside. Is the p99 due to tail queuing or kernel scheduling?
[01:44] Jordan Miles: early signs point to queueing + occasional kernel stalls when multiple requests need big kv cache reads and the runtime schedules large matmul kernels. There's also some variance in request sizes — long sequences amplify the stall.
[01:58] Alex Chen: important question — what's your target concurrency in production? Priya?
[02:02] Priya Patel: we target around 24 concurrent model streams for payments path during peak, but end-to-end request rate varies. If we can hit stable throughput at 24 with p99 under 500ms, we can move forward.
[02:12] Liam O'Connor: we also want to avoid large queues because our front-end has a small buffer. So backpressure is real.
[02:18] Jordan Miles: two levers we suggested: 1) tuning the batching window (trade latency for throughput) and 2) adding a soft concurrency cap with queueing and early reject/graded fallback to a smaller model variant for overflow.
[02:29] Sara Mu: on fallback — we'd like to see typical degrade modes, like fall back to a quantized 4-bit variant with slightly lower quality vs full model. Do you have data on accuracy loss?
[02:39] Alex Chen: we do have Redwood Optimize recommendations — Jordan can share a small eval comparing outputs on your prompt set, but we should be mindful that's a separate eval. For throughput immediate wins are batching and cache warmup.
[02:52] Jordan Miles: I ran a short test with a 10ms vs 20ms window: 10ms bias has lower latency but less effective batching so tokens/sec drops ~15%. 20ms gives the best throughput but adds ~20-30ms on average. For your SLO p99 we might need to target 15ms or pair 20ms with a concurrency cap.
[03:10] Priya Patel: hmm 15ms might be a good compromise. But that still doesn't explain the p99 spikes — any scheduling knobs we can flip on the runtime side?
[03:19] Jordan Miles: there are kernel selection heuristics and also pinning CPUs for the host process to reduce OS preemption. I suspect some background housekeeping IO kicked in during the 32-concurrency run. I'll check the host metrics.
[03:30] Liam O'Connor: can you also share the raw traces? The ones you shared looked sampled — we need full traces for 48h to catch intermittent system tasks.
[03:37] Jordan Miles: yup will do. I'll attach the full log bundle.
[03:40] Alex Chen: also worth discussing Dedicated pool sizing — if you go dedicated you can avoid noisy neighbors and reserve more predictable capacity. Priya, is dedicated on the table?
[03:49] Priya Patel: likely yes for PCI flow if numbers look good. But we need cost visibility for dedicated vs hosted. Also compliance questions around VPC and audit logs — your security doc covers that right?
[03:59] Alex Chen: yes SSO/SAML, audit logs, KMS are covered in the Private/Dedicated docs. I'll send the security pack again.
[04:05] Sara Mu: back to throughput — Jordan you mentioned cache warmup 70% hit rate. How long to warm? Our traffic shape might have cold-starts.
[04:12] Jordan Miles: on our tests warmup stabilized after ~90 seconds of sustained traffic for the prefix caches. If your traffic has lots of random prefixes warmup will be slower. We can pre-populate common prefixes if you can share a top-k prompt set.
[04:24] Priya Patel: yes we'll share top 200 prompt patterns, that's in the action items.
[04:29] Jordan Miles: cool. A second note: queueing policy. We tried an LIFO vs FIFO queue and saw slightly better p99 with LIFO for our workload because recent requests share cache state — but LIFO increases tail variance for some clients.
[04:43] Liam O'Connor: LIFO worries me because of fairness — might starve older requests if something weird happens. I'd prefer bounded FIFO + early fallback.
[04:50] Jordan Miles: that's fair. We can prototype bounded FIFO with a small overflow ring that redirects to quantized model.
[04:57] Alex Chen: action recap — Jordan to run the broader concurrency sweep up to 64 and include host-level CPU/disk metrics; Priya to send production distribution; Alex to price dedicated options.
[05:07] Sara Mu: question: any change to tokenization or batching affecting QA? We had some noisy outputs during batched runs in last POC.
[05:15] Jordan Miles: batching shouldn't change model outputs unless we change prompt concatenation or batching semantics. Our runtime preserves request separation; if you saw output mixing it's likely an instrumentation bug — I didn't observe mixing in these runs.
[05:27] Priya Patel: ok good. Could we do a 48-hour run at concurrency 24 with 15ms window and prefix pre-population? That might be our sweet spot.
[05:34] Jordan Miles: yes we can schedule that — it'll take about 48h and we'll upload raw logs.
[05:38] Alex Chen: scheduling note — we'll need your approval for sustained test traffic if you have any rate limits in the payment path.
[05:44] Priya Patel: we'll open the ticket and allocate a test window.
[05:47] Liam O'Connor: another quick ask — please include p50/p95/p99 and queue-length histogram per minute so we can see correlated spikes.
[05:55] Jordan Miles: noted. I'll include minute resolution histograms and kernel event markers.
[06:00] Alex Chen: let's talk autoscaling a bit — with Dedicated you can set a minimum pool size that prevents cold-starts; also use burst capacity for peaks. There's a cost tradeoff.
[06:09] Priya Patel: want to see cost per sustained throughput and cost per peak. That spreadsheet you promised last week will help.
[06:15] Alex Chen: re-share will be in next steps.
[06:18] Sara Mu: technical deep-dive question — are you able to pin GPU SM freq or change CUDA launch parameters? We sometimes tune kernel configs on our infra.
[06:27] Jordan Miles: on hosted we can't change physical GPU params but on Dedicated we can apply kernel-level flags and different optimized kernels. It's part of the Dedicated value prop.
[06:36] Priya Patel: good to know. If we go Dedicated we may want to test 4-bit quantized kernels and compare accuracy/throughput.
[06:42] Jordan Miles: yep we can run three variants in the same Dedicated pool if you want A/B comparison: full fp16, 8-bit, and 4-bit quantized.
[06:51] Liam O'Connor: how long does kernel selection and compilation take? We have short-lived instances sometimes.
[06:56] Jordan Miles: compilation is fast for standard models but cold-start time includes some jit and kernel warmup; Dedicated with pinned pool avoids repeated compilation.
[07:04] Alex Chen: circling back — main asks we've captured. Any blockers from customer side?
[07:09] Priya Patel: just getting the production traces and the ticket for test windows. We can do that this week.
[07:14] Sara Mu: timeline looks good. We'll review Jordan's logs when uploaded.
[07:17] Alex Chen: perfect. Quick recap items and owners — Jordan will run the 1-64 concurrency sweep and 48h run at concurrency 24 with 15ms window once Priya opens the test window; Priya to supply traces and top-k prompts; Alex to send cost/dedicated spreadsheet and security pack.
[07:33] Jordan Miles: I'll also check for background IO spikes and include host metrics — cpu, iowait, scheduling events.
[07:40] Priya Patel: thanks.
[07:42] Alex Chen: anything else?
[07:44] Liam O'Connor: no, good sync.
[07:46] Alex Chen: OK we'll follow up via email and Slack, Jordan will upload results, and we'll reconvene next week unless we hit something earlier. Thanks all.
[07:55] (call ends)
